003422eb51a309:
A language with more than a million and a half speakers

Nahuatl (or Nāhuatl) is the Indigenous language with the most speakers in Mexico: according to the 2020 INEGI census, more than 1.5 million people speak it today, mainly in Puebla, Veracruz, Hidalgo, San Luis Potosí, Guerrero and the State of Mexico. It isn't "the language of the Aztecs" in the past tense — it's a living language, with new speakers born every day, contemporary literature, music, and even content on social media.

Classical Nahuatl vs. modern variants

It's important to be honest from the start: Nahuatl isn't a single, uniform language. There are several regional variants with real differences in pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar — Huasteca Nahuatl, Sierra de Puebla Nahuatl, Isthmus Nahuatl, among others — in addition to Classical Nahuatl (the one spoken in Tenochtitlan in the 16th century, and the best documented in writing).

💡 This course uses central/classical Nahuatl as its base — it's the variant taught by most of the available teaching material, and the one that serves as the most solid starting point for beginners. If your goal is to speak with a specific community, the pronunciation and some words may vary — it's worth confirming with local speakers.

What you'll achieve in this course (level A1)

  • Correctly pronounce Nahuatl's own sounds (class 2)
  • Greet people and introduce yourself (class 3)
  • Use personal pronouns (class 4)
  • Count from 1 to 20 (class 5)
  • Talk about your family using possession (class 6)
  • Correctly name objects and people (class 7)
  • Conjugate basic verbs in the present tense (class 8)
  • Put together simple, complete dialogues (class 9)

Good news first

Most Nahuatl letters are pronounced the same as in Spanish: a, e, i, o, c, m, n, p, t... The challenge lies in a handful of specific combinations. Master them and you'll be able to read almost any word in Nahuatl.

The key sounds

SpellingSounds likeExample
tlA single sound (not "tee-ell") — the tongue touches the palate and air is released from the sidesatl (water)
x"sh" in English (shoe)xochitl (flower) → "shochitl"
hu / uh"w" in English (water)huitzilin (hummingbird) → "witzilin"
cu / uc"kw" (queen)cualli (good) → "kwalli"
llTwo "l" sounds in a row, NOT like the Spanish "y" soundcalli (house) → "cal-li"
hA soft aspiration (like a very light "h") or a brief pausenehua (I)
🎯 Practice out loud: atl (water), xochitl (flower), calli (house), cualli (good). Repeat them several times — Nahuatl pronunciation is learned with the mouth, not just the eyes.
💡 Stress in Nahuatl almost always falls on the second-to-last syllable, just like most words in Spanish ("casa," "mesa"): xo-CHI-tl, ca-LLI.

13e76fa6304962:
Your first words

NahuatlEnglish
Cualli tonalliGood day (literally: "good sun/day")
Quen tinemi?How are you? (literally: "how do you live?")
Cualli, tlazohcamatiGood, thank you
TlazohcamatiThank you
XimopanoltiWelcome (literally: "please come in")
Ma cualliThat's fine / agreed

Why "how do you live?" instead of "how are you?"

Nahuatl builds many expressions differently from Spanish/English, and translating them word for word helps you understand their internal logic. Quen tinemi comes from quen (how) + ti- (you) + nemi (to live/exist) — literally "how you live." You'll see the prefix ti- again in the next class: it's the pronoun "you" attached directly to the verb.

🎯 Simple dialogue:
A: Cualli tonalli. Quen tinemi?
B: Cualli, tlazohcamati. Ihuan tehua?
A: Cualli no.
(Good day. How are you? — Good, thank you. And you? — Good too.)
💡 Ihuan means "and" — useful for connecting phrases, as in "ihuan tehua?" (and you?).

1a5d6d93387b82:
The independent pronouns

NahuatlEnglishVerb prefix
Nehua(tl)Ini-
Tehua(tl)Youti-
Yehua(tl)He / she(none)
Tehuan(tin)Weti-...-h
Amehuan(tin)You allan-...-h
Yehuan(tin)They(none)...-h

The key: Nahuatl is an "agglutinative" language

Unlike Spanish/English, in Nahuatl the pronoun almost always attaches directly to the verb as a prefix, instead of being a separate word. That's why "I live" isn't said as "nehua nemi" in natural speech — it's simply ninemi (ni- + nemi). The independent pronoun (nehua, tehua...) is mainly used for emphasis, like saying "I, on the other hand, live here."

🎯 The verb nemi (to live/exist) conjugated:
  • Ninemi — I live
  • Tinemi — you live
  • Nemi — he/she lives
  • Tinemih — we live
  • Annemih — you all live
  • Nemih — they live
💡 Notice the pattern: singular with no -h at the end, plural WITH -h at the end. It's one of the most consistent rules in Nahuatl.

A base-20 system

Unlike Spanish/English (base 10), classical Nahuatl traditionally counts in base 20 (vigesimal) — probably because finger and toe digits were counted together. The number 20 has its own word: cempohualli (literally "one complete count"). From 11 to 19 it's built by adding on top of 10 (mahtlactli):

🎯 From 11 to 20:
  • 11 = Mahtlactli once ce (10 + 1)
  • 15 = Mahtlactli once macuilli (10 + 5)
  • 20 = Cempohualli
💡 You don't need to memorize the entire vigesimal system in this introductory course — what matters is recognizing that it exists, and mastering 1 through 10, the base for everything else.

NahuatlEnglish

Putting it together: my mother, your father

When a noun carries a possessive prefix, it generally loses its absolutive suffix (you'll see this in the next class) — so "nantli" (mother) becomes nonan (my mother), not "nonantli."

🎯 Examples:
  • Nonan = my mother
  • Motah = your father
  • Inan = his/her mother
  • Toicniuh = our sibling
💡 Don't worry about memorizing every spelling-change exception right now — the general pattern (possessive prefix + root, without the absolutive suffix) is what you need to recognize at this level.

0c0cb11f0baa2c:
What the "absolutive suffix" is

You've already seen words like atl (water), calli (house) and conetl (child). That ending isn't part of the word's root — it's the absolutive suffix, which marks that a noun is in its "free" or "unpossessed" form (it doesn't belong to anyone in the sentence). That's why, as you saw in the previous class, this suffix disappears when the noun carries a possessive prefix (nantli → nonan).

The 3 main forms

SuffixWhen it appearsExample
-tlRoot ends in a vowela + tl = atl (water)
-tliRoot ends in a consonantcal + li = calli (house)
-inSome roots (common with animals)mich + in = michin (fish)
🎯 More examples to recognize the pattern:
  • Tetl = stone
  • Xochitl = flower
  • Citlalin = star
  • Cihuatl = woman
💡 You don't need to predict which suffix each new word carries — that comes with vocabulary and practice. What matters at this level is recognizing WHAT that ending is when you see it, so you don't mistake it for part of the root.

1c786d0caa734d:
The pattern you already know, applied to more verbs

In class 4 you conjugated nemi (to live). The same prefix pattern (ni-/ti-/Ø/ti...-h/an...-h/Ø...-h) applies to most Nahuatl verbs in the present tense. Let's practice with two more verbs: choca (to cry) and tlacua (to eat).

🎯 Choca (to cry):
  • Nichoca — I cry
  • Tichoca — you cry
  • Choca — he/she cries
  • Tichocah — we cry
  • Anchocah — you all cry
  • Chocah — they cry
🎯 Tlacua (to eat):
  • Nitlacua — I eat
  • Titlacua — you eat
  • Tlacua — he/she eats
  • Titlacuah — we eat
  • Antlacuah — you all eat
  • Tlacuah — they eat

The trick for recognizing the pattern

Notice that the prefix (ni-, ti-, an-...) always goes at the START of the verb, and the plural suffix -h always goes at the END — no matter what the verb's root is. Once you memorize this "template," you can conjugate hundreds of new verbs just by knowing their root.

💡 This is the same "agglutinative language" principle you saw with the pronouns: instead of separate words (like "I" + "eat" in English), Nahuatl packs all the information into a single word.

0b358acfc71f35:
Everything you now know

Over 8 classes you learned pronunciation, greetings, pronouns, numbers, family, nouns and basic verbs. That's enough for a first real dialogue:

🎯 Complete dialogue:
A: Cualli tonalli! Quen tinemi?
B: Cualli, tlazohcamati. Ihuan tehua?
A: Cualli no. Ac timotoca? (what's your name?)
B: Nehua nimotoca Ana. Ihuan tehua?
A: Nehua nimotoca Carlos. Nican nonan ihuan notah. (Here are my mother and my father.)
B: Ximopanolti! (Welcome!)

What this course did NOT cover (and why)

This is an introductory A1 course — we didn't cover past/future tenses, the full vigesimal system, honorifics (-tzin), or classical writing with all its historical spelling variants. That belongs to a next level (A2), once this foundation is solid.

How to keep learning

  • Practice out loud every day, even if it's just 5 minutes
  • Look for real communities and speakers — Nahuatl is best learned in live conversation
  • Come back to this course and review: spaced repetition works better than rushing
💡 Tlazohcamati for making it this far — learning the first steps of a new language, especially one with a structure so different from Spanish/English, is a real achievement.
